title: 7 Softgen Alternatives Worth Trying in 2026
summary: Softgen alternatives compared by where your app's database lives: Meku, Dyad, Rocket.new, Leap.new, Blink and Fabricate, with prices and exit routes.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Three of the six tools after ours, Meku, Dyad and Rocket.new, keep your app's data in an account you own, usually Supabase or Neon.
- Softgen's Starter plan costs $25 a month with no annual option, and its 75-credit trial can't publish or push to GitHub.
- Leap.new hosts your database on Encore's cloud by default, and putting it on your own AWS or GCP needs a paid Encore Cloud Pro subscription on top of the cloud bill.
- Blink and Fabricate keep the database on their own platforms by default: Blink exports it as CSV or JSON, while code exported from Fabricate needs some setup to run on your Cloudflare account and leaves your live data behind.


Softgen's homepage makes ownership its pitch: "You Own the Code. The Database. The Hosting. All of It." You describe an app in plain English, pick a model, and get a Next.js app on Supabase that deploys to Vercel. Most Softgen alternatives lists skip the question that pitch raises, so this one answers it for every tool: where does your database live, and how do your code and data get out?


[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) is listed first because it's our product. We grouped the remaining six by where each vendor's docs put the database: tools that keep it only in an account you own, then one that hosts it by default with your own cloud as an option, then two that keep it on their own platform. Inside a group, the cheapest paid plan billed monthly goes first, and a tie goes alphabetical.


We read every plan, price and database doc quoted here on November 13, 2026, on the vendors' own sites.


## Why people look past Softgen


Softgen is live: its status page showed every service online on the day we checked. People shop around because of what each plan leaves out, and because Softgen's own documents disagree.


### Credits and models are split by plan


Starter costs $25 a month and comes with 500 credits; Pro costs $49 and comes with 1,500. Softgen's FAQ calls its credit costs "estimates rather than fixed charges": about 5 credits for a quick edit, 30 for a full page build and 50 for a refactor on a premium model. Top-ups cost $5 for 500 credits, $9 for 1,000 or $20 for 2,500.


Starter also limits you to GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, while Claude and the rest of the "12+ AI models" sit on Pro. Only Pro lists credit rollover, for one month, and only Pro adds custom domains, though the FAQ says credits don't expire while you're subscribed.


### The trial stops before launch


New accounts start with 75 credits and no card. The homepage says to "Upgrade to Starter when you want GitHub, publishing, and full model choice", so you can't push the trial's code to a repo or put it live.


Even on a paid plan, hosting isn't a line item. Softgen deploys to Vercel, on your own Vercel account or through its one-click publish, and its Academy FAQ says hosting for production "isn't directly included".


### Docs that disagree with the pricing page


Softgen's Academy help docs still describe a $33-a-year Annual Membership, and its Terms, dated August 14, 2025, still require an annual membership, though the pricing page no longer sells one. The Academy also still says Softgen builds on Firebase, while today's stack is Next.js and Supabase, and the pricing card gives Starter 10 projects where the FAQ says 7.


The membership was real. In a[Reddit thread on r/lovable](https://www.reddit.com/r/lovable/comments/1jhzf8z/we_got_a_competitor_of_lovable_now_softgen/) , one user's two comments from September 1, 2025 praised it: "you pay a small annual membership to get in the door then everything is basically wholesale cost". It's an anecdote, and Softgen's changelog fills in the dates: the membership launched August 14, 2025 and was still sold in January 2026, so the monthly plans are newer than that.


Softgen also courts Lovable users directly, with an Academy guide to importing Lovable projects, so if Lovable is the tool you're really weighing, our[Lovable alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/lovable-alternatives) roundup covers it.


## The best Softgen alternatives


The last column answers the database part of Softgen's ownership pitch for each tool, from the vendor's own docs. For reference, Softgen's answer is a Softgen-managed Supabase database, or your own Supabase project.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


A tool that keeps the database in your account gives you a second account to run, while one that keeps it on its own platform decides how your data leaves.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Teams running several agents on one app


**Overview:** We publish no database product, so we don't replace the managed Supabase that Softgen sets up for you.


What we add is several agents side by side: our homepage demo shows Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode working in parallel on one project, and our launch post says each gets its own chat on the same project files. Our docs also say a lead agent can split a job across a team of agents.


Behind each project sits its own cloud computer with storage for up to 1 TB, and our agents install and run real programs there. We're backed by Y Combinator.


**Key features:**


- Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI models, with open-source GLM and Kimi, on one bill.
- Keys added once to a shared team keychain, which teammates' agents use without anyone seeing the value.
- Connections to Slack, Notion, Figma and Stripe, plus your own MCP servers.
- Approved models and budgets set per person by an admin.


**Pricing:** Basic, the Agentic plan we'd pick for a Softgen user, costs $99 a person a month; Light is $19, Pro $199 and Studio $499. Each figure is also that person's AI budget for the month. A developer comes on the Dedicated expert plan, bought separately and priced on a call, and it includes one Light subscription.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** A cloud computer per project that runs agents unattended, a live link in one click, model and budget controls per person


**Cons:** No database product, managed auth or per-app hosting limits published, no published repo sync (GitHub connects as an app) or one-click code export (you can download files and AI Output, code included, for 30 days after canceling), a Platform Fee that lifts the real floor far above Softgen's $25, no native mobile app builds from the agents (mobile app development sits on the Dedicated expert plan), no free plan or free trial, and monthly-only Agentic plans with no refunds or budget rollover


**How to start using it:**


1. Book the Dedicated expert call first if you want a developer on the code; otherwise choose Basic.
2. Read the checkout total, fee included, before paying.
3. Describe the app in the first chat.
4. Open a second agent's chat for a parallel job, such as tests.
5. Publish the site to a live link, then send the project link to whoever reviews it.


**Why it's a good Softgen alternative:** Agents from four vendors work on one project at once, and on the separate Dedicated expert plan you hand work to a developer from the same chat.


**Final verdict:** If you build alone and want the database in your own account, Meku, Dyad or Rocket.new fits better for far less. Awesomic fits a team that wants several agents on one project, plus a vetted developer on a separate plan.


[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Basic to put several agents on one project.


### 2. Meku


**Overview:** Meku builds full-stack web apps and sites with a React, Vite and Tailwind front end and a Supabase backend. You click Connect Supabase to link your own project, and "Meku automatically maps your Supabase credentials to environment variables when you export."


Meku also hosts the front end for you: "Publish to a free meku.app subdomain or connect your own domain. Hosting and SSL are included." Its code ownership page promises code "that you fully own", downloadable as a ZIP or pushed to GitHub, and you can deploy it to Vercel, Netlify or your own servers.


**Key features:**


- One-click publishing to meku.app or a custom domain.
- Figma import and website cloning as starting points.
- An MCP server, so you can drive Meku from Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT or Codex.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 100 credits a month on its pricing card, 150 in its FAQ, and three public projects. Starter is $16 a month, or $12 a month billed yearly, for 800 credits and 20 projects, Pro is $25 or $19, and Growth is $49 or $39.


**Pros:** Your own Supabase project from Starter, hosting and SSL included, the cheapest paid plan here, billed monthly or yearly


**Cons:** Export, GitHub and Supabase all start on Starter, free projects are always public, a Vite single-page app rather than Next.js, so a Softgen project won't map across one to one


**Where it wins on ownership:** Credentials move into your exported code automatically, so the copy you take away already points at your own database.


**Final verdict:** Choose Meku if you want a hosted app with the data in your own Supabase project for the least money.


### 3. Dyad


**Overview:** Dyad answers the database question most directly. Clicking Connect Supabase opens your browser so you pick your own Supabase organization, and its docs add: "Only you can access your Supabase resources through Dyad." Neon works the same way over OAuth, for Next.js and Vite projects.


Dyad runs as a desktop app on macOS and Windows, with "experimental Linux support", and its core is open source under Apache 2.0. Each app is "just a regular Git repo on your computer", with a Sync to GitHub button. Unlike Meku, Dyad has no hosting of its own, so its docs walk you through GitHub and Vercel.


**Key features:**


- Any model through your own API key or a ChatGPT subscription.
- Supabase or Neon backends, sign-in included.
- Smart Context on Pro for large codebases.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0, needs no sign-up and runs on your own API key. Pro is $20 a month with 200 AI credits and Max is $79 a month with 900, with no annual price, and using a ChatGPT subscription in Agent mode carries "a small orchestration fee ... up to 1.5 credits per million tokens".


**Pros:** The database sits in an account only you control, code lives on your own disk, a free tier with your own key


**Cons:** JavaScript apps only, no native mobile apps, you wire up Vercel, the database and your keys yourself


**What it keeps from Softgen:** The Supabase backend and a Git repo, without a platform between you and either one.


**Final verdict:** Choose Dyad if you're comfortable running a desktop app and want nothing about your app held in someone else's account.


### 4. Rocket.new


**Overview:** Rocket.new sells three things on one credit pool: research, building and monitoring, which it calls "Vibe Solutioning". Its Build side makes websites, web apps and mobile apps, in Next.js or Flutter, and Supabase connects over OAuth: "It is the foundational backend for most Rocket apps."


Rocket hosts the app too, and its credits doc says compute, storage and hosting aren't billed separately. Its GitHub rules are the catch. Code sync needs Pro or above. It's two-way only for Next.js TypeScript, with a rocket-update branch and an automatic pull request to main, while "For all other frameworks, sync is one-way (push only)."


**Key features:**


- Next.js web apps and Flutter mobile apps from the same account.
- A screenshot or a Next.js TypeScript GitHub repo as a starting point.
- Unlimited team members on paid plans (Free caps invites at 10 people).


**Pricing:** Free is a one-time grant of 20 credits. Pro is $25 a month, or $20 a month billed yearly, for 100 credits, Rocket is $50 or $40 for 250, and Booster is $250 or $200 for 1,500, with credits rolling over while your plan is active.


**Pros:** The database stays in your Supabase account, no separate hosting charge, credits that carry over month to month


**Cons:** GitHub sync is paid and two-way only for Next.js TypeScript, Supabase is a second account with its own bill


**Why Softgen users try it:** Next.js with your own Supabase is close to Softgen's stack, and Flutter adds a mobile build that Softgen's homepage and pricing page don't describe.


**Final verdict:** Choose Rocket.new if you want Softgen's Next.js and Supabase pairing plus a mobile build, and push-only sync on the Flutter side is fine.


### 5. Leap.new


**Overview:** Leap.new is an AI developer agent from Encore, its parent company, and it builds backend-heavy apps on the open-source Encore.ts framework. It generates services, APIs, databases and infrastructure as code, and its homepage promises "Built-in PostgreSQL databases".


Where that database runs is your choice: "you can choose to deploy to a free Encore Cloud-hosted environment or connect your own AWS or GCP account." The free environment "comes with usage limits", and your own cloud "requires an Encore Cloud Pro subscription", which costs $49 per member and $99 per environment a month, plus $2.50 per resource, with AWS or GCP billing you for usage.


**Key features:**


- GitHub integration on every app.
- Architecture and service-catalog views of what the agent built.
- Import of an existing database by connection string.


**Pricing:** Leap.new's pricing page now sits behind a sign-in, so these figures come from its docs. Free gives you 15 credits a month, five a day, and Pro starts at $30 a month for 100 credits, rising to $750 for 2,500, with Team plans from $500 a month.


**Pros:** The option of a Postgres database in your own AWS or GCP account, infrastructure as code you can read, GitHub on every app


**Cons:** Pitched at professional developers in its docs, even though the homepage now says no coding is required, your own cloud means a second subscription plus the cloud bill, no annual price and a pricing page behind a sign-in (prices are in its docs)


**Its edge for this job:** It writes infrastructure as code along with the app, so putting the database in your own cloud is a deployment choice rather than a rebuild.


**Final verdict:** Choose Leap.new if you're a developer and the backend, not the screens, is the hard part of your app.


### 6. Blink


**Overview:** Blink takes the opposite approach to Dyad: its Blink Cloud bundles the database, sign-in, storage and hosting. "Your database is powered by Turso (a SQLite-compatible database) hosted on AWS edge infrastructure", per its docs, which add that you can "Export your data anytime as CSV or JSON."


Code is easier to take with you. GitHub sync is "Available on every plan, Free included", and it runs both ways, so you can "Pull changes made outside Blink" and keep editing in your own tools.


**Key features:**


- A database and sign-in on every plan, Free included.
- Two-way GitHub sync with auto-sync.
- Blink Claw, agents that run 24/7, from Starter.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 5 credits a day, up to 30 a month, on public projects. Starter is $25 a month, or $13 a month billed yearly, for 100 credits a month plus 5 a day, Pro is $50 or $25, and production hosting is paid in credits, with 50 a month covering up to 10,000 visits.


**Pros:** No Supabase or Vercel account to set up, two-way GitHub sync on Free, data export at any time


**Cons:** Hosting draws on your credits, downloading the code takes 5 credits on Starter or Pro, data leaves as CSV or JSON tables rather than a Postgres dump


**What you give up for convenience:** By default your data lives in Blink's database, so leaving means rebuilding tables elsewhere from the export, unless you connected your own Supabase project.


**Final verdict:** Choose Blink if you'd rather not run a database account at all.


### 7. Fabricate


**Overview:** Fabricate builds web apps for small businesses, such as bookings, orders and client portals, and keeps the backend inside each one. Its own Softgen comparison says it "writes the database, sign-in and server routes into the app's own code and serves each app as its own Cloudflare Worker", with "its own SQLite database".


That page ranked first for this search when we checked, so read it as a vendor's pitch. It also notes that an imported Softgen project keeps its Supabase database. Fabricate's export docs say the exported code can run on your own Cloudflare account once you add your own build step and Workers configuration, and exporting doesn't move your live data.


**Key features:**


- Stripe and transactional emails built in.
- An undo for changes to your live app's data.
- Import of Next.js projects from a public GitHub link or a .zip file, which then run as client-rendered React.


**Pricing:** Free gives you 60 credits a month and one app online for 30 days. Pro costs $20 a month on a yearly plan, or $25 month to month, and brings 350 credits, any number of live apps and up to three people. Max is $100, or $80 billed yearly, for 1,750 credits.


**Pros:** A documented import path for a Softgen-style Next.js repo, no outside database account for apps you start there, credit packs that never expire


**Cons:** Free apps go offline after 30 days, code download and GitHub only on Pro and Max, apps made on or after November 11, 2026 go offline 30 days after a downgrade to Free


**Why it's a good Softgen alternative:** It takes your existing Next.js code as a starting point, so you don't rebuild from a prompt.


**Final verdict:** Choose Fabricate if you run a small business, want the whole app hosted for you, and plan to stay on a paid plan.


## Who owns the app you generate


Softgen's pitch splits ownership into three parts, and each one has its own test. For code, ask whose GitHub account holds the repo: Softgen's Academy describes adding you to the project's repository as a collaborator. For the database, ask whose account it sits in, and for hosting, whose bill pays for it.


"You own the code" on a builder's site is a contract term, and copyright adds a limit. In[Thaler v. Perlmutter](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2025/03/23-5233.pdf) , the D.C. Circuit ruled on March 18, 2025 that "the Copyright Act requires all work to be authored in the first instance by a human being." The case concerned an image claimed with an AI system as its sole author, not every AI-assisted work, and this isn't legal advice.


The code itself may travel well. A preregistered experiment by[Borg and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00788) , with 151 participants (75 in the phase where others evolved the code), mostly professional developers, found no significant differences in completion time or code quality when others later evolved AI-assisted code, though the sample was too small to rule out modest effects. It used one Java web app and assistants like Copilot, not apps from prompt-only builders, so treat it as a hint.


If the code moves easily, the database and hosting are where leaving gets hard. One r/lovable poster[planning to leave Lovable](https://www.reddit.com/r/lovable/comments/1t994qr/i_think_its_time_to_leave_lovable/) in May 2026 wrote: "I fear they will go out of business and take my app and db along with them." The top practical reply, one Reddit user's anecdote, was to connect GitHub, open your own Supabase account and deploy through Vercel.


That's why the database decision belongs in your[SaaS product development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/saas-product-development) plan before the first prompt, not after the first paying customer.


## What leaving each tool looks like


An exit has two halves, the code and the data, and they rarely leave on the same terms. Softgen sits in the first row as the baseline.


Tool Code out Database out Plan you need


Softgen The project's GitHub repo, with you added as a collaborator Bring your own Supabase and "migrate in or out" Starter, $25 a month


Awesomic Our Terms assign you our rights in AI Output once a billing cycle is paid; files downloadable for 30 days after canceling; no repo sync published No database product published Any Agentic plan, plus the Platform Fee

The "Already" rows are the easy exits, because the data never left your account. On Softgen's side, its FAQ says that if you cancel, your app keeps running. If you're leaving Bolt.new rather than Softgen, the same code-and-data checks apply, and our[Bolt.new alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/bolt-new-alternatives) roundup compares where its users go.


## Softgen competitors we left off this list


Other Softgen lists name Lovable, Bolt.new, v0 and Base44, and we left them out because our blog already reviews each at length. Of the four, v0 is closest to Softgen's stack, Next.js on Vercel, and our[v0 alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/v0-alternatives) roundup sets it against its rivals.


## How to choose a Softgen alternative


Start from the database question, then the price. These pairings follow the groups above:


- If you want hosting handled but the data in your own Supabase project, Meku's Starter covers both.
- If you want the database in your own account and the code on your own disk, start with Dyad's free tier.
- If you need a mobile app too, Rocket.new builds Flutter apps alongside Next.js.
- If the backend is the hard part and you may move to AWS or GCP later, try Leap.new.
- If you'd rather never open Supabase or Vercel, Blink or Fabricate hosts the app and the data.
- If you want several agents on one project and a developer on a separate expert plan, that's the job we built Awesomic for.


If you need a native mobile app rather than a web app, our[Rork alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/rork-alternatives) roundup covers builders made for that.


## Run an exit test before you commit


Before you move a real project, build a throwaway app on your top two picks with a sign-in and one table of data. Push the code to GitHub, export the data, and deploy the code somewhere the vendor doesn't control, then time each step.


If what you need is a marketing site rather than an app,[web design by vetted designers](https://www.awesomic.com/web-design) may suit you better than any builder here.


## FAQ


### Does Softgen have a free plan?


No, but it has a trial: new accounts get 75 credits with no card. The trial doesn't include GitHub or publishing, which start on Starter at $25 a month, and the full model list starts on Pro at $49. Meku's own Softgen comparison still says Softgen offers no trial, which is out of date.


### Does Softgen still use Firebase?


No. Softgen's homepage lists Next.js, Supabase, Vercel, GitHub, Stripe and Resend as its core stack. Its Academy docs and Rocket.new's own Softgen roundup still say Firebase, and both are out of date.


### Which Softgen alternatives host the app and database for you?


Blink and Fabricate host both for apps you build there, with no outside account. Meku and Rocket.new host the app but keep the database in your own Supabase, and Leap.new offers a free Encore Cloud environment with usage limits. If Base44 is also on your list, our[Base44 alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/base44-alternatives) roundup weighs the same trade for its users.


### Can I move a Softgen project to another builder?


Yes, if you're on a paid plan. Your code sits in a GitHub repo you can clone, and Fabricate says it can bring in a Next.js project from a public GitHub link or from a zipped copy, so zip a private repo first. If you brought your own Supabase project, the data is already yours, and Softgen's changelog says you can migrate in or out.


### Which Softgen alternative is cheapest?


Every alternative here except ours has a $0 tier, and Dyad's runs on your own API key, so you pay your model provider instead of buying credits. Among the paid plans of the six tools after ours, Meku's Starter is the lowest on both billing options, $16 a month or $12 a month billed yearly, against Softgen's $25 Starter.
